items.prompt: What makes a complexity explanation defensible?

options.text: It identifies the input variables, cost model, executed operations, and how their counts compose.
It names a familiar Big-O class without justification.
It counts loop keywords.
It interprets variable names as complexity annotations.

feedback.reason: A good explanation connects program behavior to an asymptotic expression.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

A reader should be able to reproduce the bound: identify independent input sizes, declare the cost of primitives and library calls, count how often each operation executes, and combine sequential, nested, recursive and output phases correctly. The final notation must also name its guarantee—worst-case, expected, amortized or output-sensitive—because those claims answer different questions.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Treat Big-O as the conclusion of a derivation. A familiar label without the workload boundary and counting argument is not yet an explanation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.label_only: A class name states the conclusion but gives no operation count, assumptions or composition that another reader can verify.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.syntax_only: Loop keywords reveal nesting shape but not bounds, shared progress, early exits or work hidden in called operations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: Identifier names do not impose iteration bounds or costs and therefore provide no complexity evidence.

items.prompt: Why is "there are two nested loops, so the algorithm is O(n²)" incomplete?

options.text: The inner bounds and whether work resets or is globally bounded must be analyzed.
Nested loops can never be quadratic.
Two loops always add to O(n).
The loop variables may not be named i and j.

feedback.reason: Nested loops multiply only when the inner work repeats independently for each outer iteration.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Multiplication is justified only when each of Θ(n) outer iterations independently performs Θ(n) inner work. If an inner pointer advances globally and never resets, its total movement across all outer iterations may be Θ(n), making aggregate work Θ(n) despite nested syntax. Conversely, two independent full scans do multiply to Θ(n²).

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Ask whether inner progress resets. Sum the actual inner iterations across the whole run instead of multiplying loop headers mechanically.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.nested_never: When the inner loop performs a full n-step scan for each of n outer iterations, the total is quadratic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.two_means_linear: Two sequential loops add, but genuinely nested independent ranges multiply; syntax alone does not choose between them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: Changing i or j cannot alter reset behavior, iteration bounds or aggregate executed work.

items.prompt: A report says a function is O(log n) because it contains a variable named mid. What is the defect?

options.text: It does not show that the remaining domain shrinks geometrically or that midpoint work is bounded.
The name mid is reserved for O(n) algorithms.
Every midpoint computation is logarithmic by definition.
The name affects space but not time.

feedback.reason: Logarithmic time comes from a geometric reduction in candidates.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

A midpoint is only a computed position. Logarithmic iteration follows when every update legally discards a constant fraction of the remaining domain: after t halvings, at most n/2^t candidates remain, and n/2^t ≤ 1 gives t ≥ log2 n. If a boundary moves by one—or fails to move—the same `mid` variable can produce linear work or nontermination.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Prove the shrink invariant and bounded work per iteration. The word `mid` is neither a correctness proof nor a complexity proof.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_reserved: No identifier is reserved for a complexity class; only executed boundary updates determine iteration count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.log_always: A midpoint calculation can be followed by a one-step shrink or no legal shrink, so logarithmic time does not follow.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.space_only: The spelling of a variable changes neither time operations nor live storage.

items.prompt: A query method is described as O(1), but building its lookup table costs O(n). What should the full one-query workload report?

options.text: O(n) total for build plus one O(1) query, unless preprocessing already exists outside the measured workload.
O(1) unconditionally.
O(n²).
O(k) for an unrelated output size.

feedback.reason: Complexity boundaries must match the workload boundary.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

If the lookup table does not already exist outside the measured request, the function performs O(n) construction followed by one O(1) lookup. Sequential phases add to O(n + 1) = O(n). Reporting O(1) is valid only for the narrower post-build query operation and must say that the preprocessing cost is excluded or shared across a larger workload.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Name the measured lifecycle: build-and-query, one query against existing state, or build amortized over q queries. Different boundaries yield different valid expressions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.query_only: This describes only the post-build primitive and omits construction required by the stated one-query workload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.multiply: The build executes once and the query follows it, so their costs add rather than multiply.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output: The workload returns one result and introduces no independent k-sized output term.

items.prompt: A function returns k records but claims O(1) time because the records were already known. What is missing?

options.text: The cost of materializing or emitting the k required records.
Nothing; known values require no output work.
A variable must be named output.
All output is automatically amortized.

feedback.reason: A constant-time discovery does not imply constant-time materialization.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Knowing where the records are may make discovery O(1), but the interface still must copy, serialize, yield or otherwise emit k records. Under a materialized result contract, that establishes Ω(k) time and usually Ω(k) output storage, or more if each record has nonconstant size. A lazy symbolic handle would be a different contract.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Separate discovery from delivery. Complexity cannot be asymptotically smaller than mandatory output work under the actual interface.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.search_only: The interface still performs at least one emission action per required record even when their locations are already known.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: Calling a variable `output` neither creates nor removes the copying and serialization operations required by the contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.amortized: Amortization redistributes cost across a defined operation sequence; it does not erase mandatory output from one request.

items.prompt: A dynamic-array append is labeled worst-case O(1) because its amortized cost is O(1). What is the correction?

options.text: A resize-triggering append can be O(n) worst-case even though a sequence of appends is O(1) amortized each.
Worst-case and amortized must always be equal.
Every append copies the whole array.
Amortized means average over random inputs.

feedback.reason: Amortized throughput does not imply a per-call latency bound.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Most appends write into existing capacity in O(1), but an append that triggers geometric growth allocates a larger buffer and copies Θ(n) existing elements. Across n appends, resize copies form a geometric sum below a constant multiple of n, yielding O(n) total and O(1) amortized per append. That aggregate guarantee does not change the Θ(n) worst-case latency of the resizing call.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Report both throughput and latency when users can observe a single operation: amortized O(1) per append, worst-case O(n) for one resize.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_constant: Amortized cost averages a deterministic sequence budget, while worst-case cost bounds one selected operation; they need not match.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_linear: Only resize-triggering appends copy existing elements; most writes use reserved capacity and take constant time.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.average_random: Amortized analysis needs no probability distribution and instead bounds total cost over every legal operation sequence.

items.prompt: Why is a library call not automatically O(1)?

options.text: The call may sort, scan, copy, allocate, or hash data proportional to input size.
All library calls are O(n²).
Parentheses make a call constant-time.
Compiled code has no asymptotic cost.

feedback.reason: Abstraction hides implementation details, not computational cost.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

One source-level call may internally scan n elements, compare and sort them, allocate a copy or hash a key whose length is m. The call boundary reduces code visible to the caller but does not collapse those operations to one unit. Use the API's documented contract or inspect the implementation and cost model relevant to the input representation.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Expand every nonprimitive operation to its asymptotic contract. Parentheses indicate invocation, not constant work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.libraries_slow: Library operations range from constant-time access to sorting or copying; their documented behavior determines the bound.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.syntax: The same call syntax can wrap constant, linear or superlinear work and therefore supplies no complexity class.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.compiled: Compilation may optimize constants but still executes input-dependent scans, comparisons, allocations and copies at runtime.

items.prompt: Two sequential loops each scan n elements. Why is O(n²) the wrong explanation?

options.text: Their costs add to 2n rather than multiplying.
Loops cost nothing when sequential.
Only the first loop counts.
The loops use different variable names.

feedback.reason: Multiplication applies to repeated nesting, while sequential phases add.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The first loop performs n iterations and finishes before the second performs another n. Sequential composition gives n + n = 2n operations, whose constant factor is dropped to O(n). Multiplication would require one n-iteration loop to run inside every iteration of the other, which is not this control flow.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Add costs for phases that run one after another; multiply only when one repeated range is executed inside another.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.loops_free: Each loop still executes n body operations, so sequential placement changes composition but does not erase their work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.one_ignored: Both phases execute and contribute to the count, even though asymptotic simplification absorbs their constant factor.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: Different iterator names do not turn sequential control flow into nesting or change either range.

items.prompt: A space explanation sums every temporary buffer ever allocated, even though their lifetimes do not overlap. What is the correction?

options.text: Use peak simultaneously live memory, taking a maximum for nonoverlapping buffers.
Keep the sum because allocation count is time.
Count only the final buffer regardless of size.
Temporary buffers are output.

feedback.reason: Space complexity measures the largest live footprint.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Suppose buffer A of size a is released before buffer B of size b is allocated. The peak attributable to these phases is max(a, b), not a + b, because both are never live simultaneously. If their lifetimes overlap, their sizes do add at the overlap. Cumulative allocation volume may matter for time or allocator pressure, but it is a different metric from peak auxiliary space.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Draw lifetimes when space terms are ambiguous. Sum simultaneous storage; take a maximum across mutually exclusive or nonoverlapping phases.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.time_sum: Counting every allocation can describe cumulative allocator work, but peak space depends on which allocations coexist.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.last_only: A released earlier buffer can still define the maximum footprint if it was larger than the final one.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_only: Temporary buffers support computation and are auxiliary storage unless the result contract returns them.

items.prompt: A recursive algorithm makes two child calls, and the explanation counts only recursion depth. What may be missing from time analysis?

options.text: The total number of calls across the recursion tree and local work per call.
Stack depth is always the complete time bound.
The child function names.
Only output size can affect recursion.

feedback.reason: Time counts every executed call, while stack space counts simultaneous depth.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

A binary recursion of depth d may contain 1 + 2 + ... + 2^d = Θ(2^d) total calls, and each call's local work contributes to time. Stack space follows only one active root-to-leaf path at once, giving O(d) frames when sibling calls complete sequentially. Depth therefore cannot substitute for the total-node count in time analysis.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Use the recursion tree or recurrence for time, and maximum active path plus per-frame state for stack space.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.stack_only_time: Depth counts one active path, while time must include calls executed in every sibling branch.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.names: Child function names provide no recurrence, branching factor or local operation count.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.output_only: Even with constant-size output, branching can execute exponentially many calls and dominate time.

items.prompt: Which elements belong in a strong complexity explanation? Select all that apply.

options.text: The input-size variables and their relationships.
The assumed cost of primitive or library operations.
How sequential, nested, recursive, and output work combine.
The semantic meaning inferred from names such as i, mid, or result.

feedback.reason: A complexity label should be reproducible from stated assumptions and executed work.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Input variables define what may grow, the cost model says what each primitive or library operation costs, and composition explains how counts add, multiply, recur or depend on output. Together they let another reader reproduce the final bound. Names such as `i`, `mid` or `result` can improve readability but impose no operational guarantee.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Accept `input_variables`, `cost_model` and `composition`; reject names because notation becomes evidence only after its behavior is defined.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.variable_names: A conventional identifier does not determine its range, update rule, called work or relationship to input size.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.cost_model: Operation cost may depend on width or data structure.

items.prompt: Which are common missing terms in complexity reports? Select all that apply.

options.text: A sort, index build, or prefix-table construction.
The number q multiplying per-query cost.
The cost and storage of k returned records.
The number of comments in source code.

feedback.reason: Reports often quote the cheapest visible phase and omit the rest of the workload.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

A query may rely on a prior sort or index build, q requests repeat the per-query term, and returning k records imposes emission time plus output storage. Omitting any of these can reduce a full workload to its cheapest visible phase and produce a misleading claim. Source comments do not execute and therefore add no runtime term.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Accept preprocessing, query multiplicity and output. Then check whether updates or representation conversion add further lifecycle terms.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.comments: Comments may document the model but do not execute operations or allocate runtime storage in the analyzed program.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.preprocessing: One-time work may dominate small workloads.

items.prompt: Which statements are false heuristics? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nested loops are always O(n²).
Using a midpoint makes time logarithmic.
Amortized O(1) equals worst-case O(1).
Sequential phases add their operation counts.

feedback.reason: Complexity must be derived from execution, not memorized visual patterns.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Nested loops may share globally bounded progress, a midpoint may fail to halve the legal domain, and an amortized sequence guarantee permits an expensive individual operation. All three visual shortcuts are therefore false. Sequential phases really do add their operation counts when each phase executes, so that statement is a valid composition rule rather than a heuristic.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Accept the three claims that infer cost from surface appearance; reject `sequential_add` because it follows directly from executed phase composition.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sequential_add: When both phases execute one after another, their operation counts do add before asymptotic simplification.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.nested_quadratic: Aggregate bounds and asymmetric dimensions can differ.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.amortized_worst: An individual operation may be expensive.

items.prompt: Which review questions help detect an invalid output-sensitive claim? Select all that apply.

options.text: How many records can the contract require?
How much representation each result requires.
Whether outputs are stored, streamed, or represented symbolically under the contract.
Whether the output loop is named emit.

feedback.reason: Output lower bounds depend on result count, representation, and interface.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

The maximum number of results and representation size per result determine how much data must be delivered. The interface then decides whether that data is retained, streamed one item at a time or represented by a legal symbolic handle. These contracts yield different peak-space bounds, although explicitly emitting k records still requires Ω(k) actions. A loop's name changes none of them.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Accept count, record size and delivery mode. Verify that a claimed lazy representation is actually permitted by the public result contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.loop_name: Renaming an emission loop neither changes how many records the contract requires nor how many bytes each contains.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.record_size: A result may contain multiple elements.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.materialized_or_streamed: The interface affects space and timing.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly separate time and space reasoning? Select all that apply.

options.text: Time counts cumulative executed work, while space usually counts peak live storage.
Recursive time may depend on all calls, while stack space depends on maximum active depth.
Output storage can be reported separately from auxiliary space.
Time and space complexities must have the same class.

feedback.reason: A sound explanation uses the correct aggregation rule for each resource.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Time accumulates all executed operations, whereas space normally measures the largest simultaneously live footprint. Recursive time can include every node while stack space includes only the deepest active path. Returned storage may be reported separately from auxiliary working memory so an output-mandated bound is not mistaken for algorithmic overhead.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Accept all three distinctions. Reject equality because the aggregation rules and roles differ even for the same execution.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_equal: An algorithm may stream exponential work with linear stack space or allocate linear state for a linear-time scan, so the classes need not match.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.calls_vs_depth: Branching and depth answer different questions.

items.prompt: Arrange the construction of a concise complexity explanation.

elements.text: State input variables, case, and primitive-operation assumptions.
Explain how many times dominant operations execute.
Include preprocessing, repeated queries, output, and peak storage where applicable.
Simplify the expression and report time, auxiliary space, and output space separately.

feedback.reason: The explanation moves from model to operations to complete workload to final notation.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Begin with the variables, case and primitive-cost model so later counts have meaning. Derive operation frequency next, then add lifecycle and output terms plus peak storage. Simplification belongs last: reducing an incomplete expression early can hide the very term that dominates the requested workload.

items: State input-size variables, bound type and primitive-operation assumptions.
Count how often the dominant operations execute.
Add preprocessing, repeated queries, output and peak-live storage where applicable.
Simplify and report time, auxiliary space and output space separately.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: The order is part of auditability: assumptions → counts → complete workload → notation. Reversing it encourages post-hoc justification of a guessed label.

items.prompt: A function sorts n records, scans them once, and returns k copied records. Select time, auxiliary space excluding the sort implementation and output, and output space.
constraints: Comparison sorting costs O(n log n).
The scan and each copied output record cost O(1).
The chosen sort uses O(1) additional working storage for this question.

feedback.reason: The sort dominates the input-processing term, and k output copies add output-sensitive work.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Sorting costs O(n log n), the scan adds O(n), and copying k records adds O(k). Sequential composition gives O(n log n + n + k) = O(n log n + k); k remains because output may not be bounded by the sorting term under the stated variables. The prompt declares constant sort working storage, so auxiliary space is O(1), while the returned copies occupy O(k) output space.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: Do not merge output into auxiliary storage. Also do not drop k unless the contract proves a relationship such as k ≤ n.

items.prompt: A dynamic array receives n appends with geometric resizing. Select total sequence cost, amortized cost per append, and worst-case cost of one append.
constraints: Copying one stored element is O(1).

feedback.reason: A complete report keeps total, amortized, and per-operation worst case distinct.

blocks.text: How to reason about it

Ordinary appends contribute n constant writes. Resize copies occur at geometrically growing capacities, so 1 + 2 + 4 + ... below n is less than 2n; total sequence work is O(n). Dividing that sequence bound across n appends gives O(1) amortized cost. A single append that triggers the largest resize still copies Θ(n) elements and is O(n) worst-case.

blocks.title: Key idea
blocks.text: These three answers describe different guarantees: total throughput, charge per operation across a sequence, and maximum latency of one call.
